about: For each school fund outside the voted budget: what came in and what went out, FY2023 to FY2026, and whether the revolving funds cover their own booked costs.

conclusions.basis: `munis-school-ytd.csv`, special-school, period 13, FY2023-FY2026 (revenue and expense per fund); balances from /analysis/sitting-on-money.
conclusions.claim: The schools’ fourteen own funds spent $1,002,938 more than came in over four years.
conclusions.detail: FY2023 to FY2026, the fourteen fee, choice, lunch, gift and circuit-breaker funds took in $8,059,022 and spent $9,061,961. Their combined balance fell from $2,170,682 at 30 June 2022 to $1,167,744 at 30 June 2026. Every kind spent more than it took in except the gift funds, which took in $21,131 more than they spent.
conclusions.not_shown: Why each fund drew down. Spending a balance down can be a plan to use accumulated fees, a fee set below cost, or one-time purchases; the ledger gives amounts, not reasons.
conclusions.so_what: That money came out of balances built up to FY2022: it was spent, not held back.

conclusions.claim: Three of the fourteen funds spent more than came in, in three of the four years.
conclusions.detail: Counted per fund, FY2023 to FY2026: a year counts when expenditure exceeded revenue. No fund did it in all four years.
conclusions.not_shown: Whether the pattern continues. Four closed years is what the ledgers cover.
conclusions.so_what: After-school activities, extended day and the circuit breaker: a pattern, not one bad year.

conclusions.claim: Extended day, minuted as self-sustaining, spent $241,062 more than it took in since FY2024.
conclusions.detail: It took in more than it spent in FY2023 and less in each of FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026. Carried forward, its balance stood at -$2,569 at 30 June 2026; that year-end is carried through the ledger, not yet checked against a second document.
conclusions.not_shown: Why: a fee held while wages rose, more staff, fewer families, or a cost recoded into the fund would all look the same here.
conclusions.so_what: Its fees stopped covering its own booked spending; it ran on its balance instead.

conclusions.basis: `munis-school-ytd.csv`: special-school fund 1301 and gf-school function 3510, period 13.
conclusions.claim: Athletics fees paid for 25.5% of the athletics spending the books show, FY2023–FY2026.
conclusions.detail: The fee fund spent $745,146 and the general fund $1,613,201 under function 3510, the only fee-funded programme where both book to the same code. In FY2025 the fee fund spent $32,796 while the general fund spent $541,945.
conclusions.not_shown: The whole cost of athletics: fields, custodians, utilities and buses booked elsewhere are not in either figure (registered gaps).
conclusions.so_what: The general fund carried most of it, under the same athletics function code.

conclusions.claim: School lunch runs on federal money: 93.8% of its receipts, against 3.8% from sales.
conclusions.detail: Four years, FY2023 to FY2026. In FY2026 it spent $380,087 more than it took in, and its balance fell to $75,039.
conclusions.not_shown: Whether FY2026’s shortfall is late reimbursement booked after the close or a real loss; nothing here separates them.
conclusions.so_what: Whether lunch “pays its own way” is a question about reimbursement, not about prices.
